Sakura Sushi / Design review
Visual identity audit · 28 October 2026
A visual & experiential audit

A little restaurant.
A clearer identity.

A guided review of the sushi game’s art, interface, menus, progression and accessibility — grounded in an actual local playthrough.

The verdict

The room has a voice.
The surrounding experience needs to catch up.

Warm wood, soft light, a familiar isometric room and expressive characters make the restaurant memorable. The biggest opportunity is to make progression as legible and visually cohesive as the room itself.

Keep

The recognizable room silhouette, gentle palette, approachable characters, clear study connection and visible upgrade effects.

Strengthen

Body-text readability, mobile shopping, the hierarchy of menus and the way a new purchase is revealed.

Reconcile

Flat project illustrations with the textured restaurant, and overlapping late-game wall and floor objects.

Priority key

P1 affects a core experience or major visual payoff; P2 improves recurring usability; P3 polishes consistency.

01 / Identity inventory

What the game is made of

The audit describes the identity that exists today, then identifies where its parts drift apart.

World & sprites

A cozy diorama

Three 1536 × 1024 room illustrations share an open-corner camera and footprint. A chef, guests, food, equipment and decorations are layered over the room; the conveyor and guests make later tiers visibly busier.

Source asset preview · chef, guest and basic nigiri
Interface language

Rustic pixel UI

Wood-textured bars, cream panels, dark stepped borders, gold accents and DotGothic16 establish a game shell. Renovation cards use a rounder, system-font treatment; menu sections also mix sprites and native emoji.

Swedish is the primary interface language; Japanese phrases, readings and translations give the restaurant a specific learning purpose.

Interaction & motion

Study, earn, build

The loop is study → unlock a purchase → collect yen → upgrade the room. Guests lead to optional Japanese practice. Chefs, plates, petals and the conveyor add life; the code includes reduced-motion rules.

The guest hit areas and accessibility labels exist, but small visual cues and dense copy can make discovery harder.

02 / Findings

Where to focus

Each finding includes an observed state, why it matters, a practical next move and links to the supporting screenshots below.

P1Art direction01

Bring optional projects into the same visual world

Observed. Build Läshörna, then compare it and all four projects against the tier-3 room. The bookcase, bunting, garden forms and lanterns use flat geometric shapes beside a textured, outlined room.

Why it matters. The most expensive cosmetic rewards feel like a different art set, and the bookcase interrupts the entrance area.

Next move. Give projects the room’s perspective, outline, shading, texture and grounded shadows. Review every project alone and in combination at all tiers.

Evidence: screen 23 · screen 24
P1Scene layering02

Give the certificate and wall decoration separate space

Observed. In a finished tier-3 profile, equip the paper lantern; then remove it. The lantern occupies the same wall area and covers part of the master certificate.

Why it matters. Two independently earned rewards obscure one another.

Next move. Reserve separate anchors for persistent achievements and the wall slot; test each wall item with the certificate at every tier.

Evidence: screen 19 · screen 22
P1Readability03

Use a readable text face and minimum size for information

Observed. Inspect the HUD, menu and shop on desktop and at 390 × 844. Small pixel text is used for prices, progress, explanations and labels. The mobile uncollected-income label measured about 9.9 CSS px.

Why it matters. Players must decipher the most important instructions and status at the smallest size.

Next move. Keep DotGothic16 for titles and short game labels; use a legible body face, larger minimum sizes, and stronger hierarchy for prices, status and explanations.

Evidence: screen 02 · screen 05 · screen 12 · screen 14
P1Mobile shopping04

Make the first filtered result visible sooner

Observed. At 390 × 844 select Dekoration. A large renovation card appears before the filtered items; the heading, filters and explanation remain above the scrolling results.

Why it matters. Players spend the first screen on context instead of the category they chose.

Next move. Hide or collapse the renovation promotion in filtered views, condense the introductory copy, and reduce the persistent header height.

Evidence: screen 13 · screen 14
P2Information architecture05

Break the long menu into named destinations

Observed. Open Meny and look for decoration slots or projects. Chapter memories and several sections precede those controls.

Why it matters. A single label hides multiple tasks and makes repeat customization feel like a hunt.

Next move. Add short section tabs or jump links for Minnen, Meny, Inredning and Projekt; place the most frequently changed choices near the top.

Evidence: screen 05 · screen 06 · screen 21
P2Preview06

Keep the object being previewed in view

Observed. Open the renovation preview. Its wide panel occupies the lower portion of the room, including much of the counter and floor.

Why it matters. The player cannot easily inspect the very change they are considering.

Next move. Move the details into a compact side panel on desktop and a collapsible bottom sheet on mobile; provide a clear before/after comparison.

Evidence: screen 08 · screen 09
P2Reward feedback07

Show the purchased change, not just the transaction

Observed. Buy the prep counter in an unlocked profile. The shop announces success, but the room is behind the modal; after closing it, the counter is a small object partly behind the chef.

Why it matters. A meaningful purchase is easy to miss even though the numeric change is clear.

Next move. Offer an unobstructed “see it in your restaurant” moment, briefly spotlight the new object and maintain a readable silhouette at each tier.

Evidence: screen 15 · screen 16
P2State clarity08

Distinguish locked, available and owned actions at a glance

Observed. In the initial shop the disabled renovation button remains a saturated red call to action, while the nearby text explains the missing medal.

Why it matters. Color and visual weight suggest an action is ready before its prerequisites are met.

Next move. Use a consistent disabled treatment plus a short explicit reason alongside the control; reserve the strongest accent for the action that can be taken now.

Evidence: screen 07 · screen 13 · screen 15
P2Navigation & affordances09

Name the icon-only controls and the guest interaction

Observed. The top bar shows icons for menu, shop and returning to study; guests have small heart markers and a low-contrast instruction below the room.

Why it matters. The controls are named in the accessibility tree, but their purpose is less obvious visually, especially on touch devices.

Next move. Add compact visible labels where space permits, use a speech cue for guests, and maintain generous tap targets. At 390 px the guest targets measured 44 × 44 CSS px; the shop button was about 46 × 38.

Evidence: screen 02 · screen 12
P2Cosmetic rewards10

Show what a project actually adds before spending

Observed. The project cards describe a library, lantern evening, Japanese garden and hanami, but show only small icons. The all-project scene renders a small party setting without the cherry trees described in the Hanami text.

Why it matters. A high-cost appearance-only reward is hard to judge and may not match the player’s mental picture.

Next move. Add in-room previews or accurate thumbnails and align descriptions with the delivered scene; make the promised focal elements visible.

Evidence: screen 06 · screen 23 · screen 24
P3Visual consistency11

Unify icon and component treatments

Observed. Compare the illustrated item sprites, native emoji in the menu and finale, pixel-framed controls, and the rounded, system-font renovation card.

Why it matters. Each part is individually understandable, but the mix weakens the game’s otherwise distinctive material language.

Next move. Define one icon family, a small set of border and corner styles, and a typography rule for display, body, status and Japanese text.

Evidence: screen 05 · screen 07 · screen 20 · screen 21
P3Numbers & copy12

Use one yen-formatting rule

Observed. The balance shows “¥ 18,740” while the renovation card shows “¥ 3 600” in the same Swedish interface.

Why it matters. The inconsistent grouping makes otherwise related amounts feel like separate systems.

Next move. Choose one locale-aware yen format and reuse it in balances, cards, goals, messages and the collection button.

Evidence: screen 02 · screen 07
03 / The walkthrough

Follow the player’s path

Every image is from this audit run. Select any screenshot to enlarge it. Some late-game states use explicitly seeded local profiles.

STEP 01

Entry & sign-in

Clear, but text-heavy

The account gate explains the study connection and offers a route back. The local test-account option is development-only.

STEP 02

The restaurant & collection

Strong core, small labels

The room immediately establishes the fantasy. The goal, balance and collection bar compete around it; the collection action updates the balance and empties the register.

STEP 03

Talk to a guest

Charming connection to study

The hearts are clickable guest affordances. A phrase, pronunciation and translation connect the scene to Japanese study.

STEP 04

Restaurant menu & projects

Useful, hard to scan

One long menu combines chapter memories, owned recipes, upgrades, decoration slots and optional projects. Customization sits well below the opening content.

STEP 05

The shop

Detailed, visually dense

The shop explains medal requirements, prices and expected effects. Category filters help, but the renovation card stays above results and the header takes substantial space on a phone.

STEP 06

Preview before buying

Good intent, uneven execution

Decoration preview places an item into the actual room. Renovation preview is useful, but its large bottom panel covers much of the scene being compared.

STEP 07

Purchase & feedback

The numbers communicate more than the scene

The disposable unlocked profile can buy a prep counter. The owned state, balance and production rate update, while the new scene object is small and partly hidden behind the chef.

STEP 08

Renovation & equipment

A satisfying visual step

Tier 2 keeps the same camera and recognizable footprint, while changing counter, stools and cabinetry. The conveyor is easy to recognize after purchase.

STEP 09

Personalization

Powerful, but buried

Owned decorations can be switched or removed. Comparing the final room with and without the lantern reveals that it overlaps the master certificate.

STEP 10

Final tier & cosmetic projects

Most in need of art direction

The final tier is a distinct room with the same spatial identity. Its optional project illustrations introduce flatter geometry and crowd the isometric scene.

STEP 11

Completion

Warm and clear

The finale celebrates seven chapters and offers both a return to study and a way to stay in the restaurant.

STEP 12

Mobile & alternate theme

Functional, but constrained

At 390 × 844, the room and guests become small while the shop header and introductory text consume a large part of the modal. The Sakura theme is most evident in the panels.

04 / Recommended sequence

Make the biggest gains first

These are design priorities, not estimates or a commitment to implement changes.

FIRST

Protect readability

Set text and target-size rules; simplify the mobile shop header and filtered results. Verify at phone sizes and zoom.

NEXT

Make rewards visible

Resolve wall overlap, preserve the room in previews, and reveal a newly purchased object in context.

THEN

Finish the art system

Rework project assets to match the room, introduce accurate previews, and document sprite, icon, typography and component rules.

05 / Evidence & limits

What was checked

A visual and interaction audit of the local implementation, supported by the relevant scene, catalog and stylesheet source.

Observed

  • Sign-in gate and local test entry; tier-1 room, goal, collection, guest phrases and practice.
  • Shop filters, locked and owned items, decoration and renovation previews, purchases, tier-2 renovation and conveyor.
  • Tier-3 completed restaurant, decoration removal, finale, one project purchase and a seeded all-project combination.
  • Desktop at 1280 × 720, phone at 390 × 844, and additional portrait captures; two interface themes.
  • Escape closed the mobile shop and focus returned to its trigger. The scene exposed a descriptive image and the guest buttons had names.

Not established

  • The Firebase-emulator preview could not start in this environment, so the audit used the local in-memory service and test profiles. Real Google sign-in, server saving and medal synchronization were not verified.
  • No full screen-reader, keyboard traversal, color-contrast, zoom, voice, reduced-motion or cross-browser audit was performed. Source includes reduced-motion styling, but that is not a live verification.
  • Not every item, error state, combination, animation frame or device was exercised; late-game fixtures are illustrative rather than natural progression.
  • Accessibility comments identify risks and observed behavior; they are not a WCAG conformance claim.

Source review: src/course/sushi-game/sushi.css, sushi-view.ts, companion-view.ts, restaurant-scene.ts, tier-scenes.ts and the project’s sprite assets.
